result.note: Tests the market-access terms, the agriculture carve-out, and the CBAM and steel outcomes of the India–EU FTA concluded in January 2026.

questions.prompt: In January 2026, India and the European Union reached political consensus on a Free Trade Agreement. Consider the following statements about it:
items: India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on 96.6% of EU goods exports by value.
The EU will cut tariffs on 99.5% of imports from India over seven years.
Agricultural products and food are carved out of the deal.
questions.ask: How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: All three are correct. The EU estimates India's cuts will save European firms about EUR 4 billion a year in duties, while its own cuts favour labour-heavy Indian exports such as textiles, leather and gems. The agriculture carve-out was meant to avoid the farmer backlash that stalled the EU's Mercosur pact.
questions.source: The EU will cut tariffs on 99.5% of imports from India over 7 years, a clear boost for textiles, leather, chemicals, gems/jewellery, and other labour-heavy items.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about the climate and steel provisions of the India–EU Free Trade Agreement concluded in January 2026:
items: India secured an exemption from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) levy.
The EU agreed to provide India with EUR 500 million in support tied to emissions cuts.
The EU agreed to allow 1.6 million metric tons of duty-free steel exports from India.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: Statement 1 is wrong. India won no leeway on the CBAM levy, only a promise to keep talking about technicalities. The EUR 500 million in support and the duty-free steel quota were what India got instead.
questions.source: The EU agreed to provide India with EUR 500 million in support tied to emissions cuts and 1.6 million metric tons of duty-free steel exports to the EU.
